entries.answer: Leadership Meet Our Chairman Olabanji O. Folayan Chairman Certified Protection Professional (CPP), ASIS Board-Certified Project Manager (CPM), IAPM B.A. in Business, M.S. in Management, and a Graduate Certificate in Homeland Security Management, University of Maryland University College CHS-V designation through the American Board of Certification in Homeland Security 23 years of experience in various security and emergency management positions Olabanji O. Folayan was born and raised in the Washington Metropolitan Area, and attended the University of the District of Columbia (B.A., Business Administration 1997) and University of Maryland (M.S. Management 2004 and Graduate Certificate in Homeland Security Management 2007). Prior to establishing Securemedy, Incorporated, Mr. Folayan worked in various capacities from security officer to management, working on commercial and government contracts. He has provided oversight for a workforce of over 300 employees. His duties included management oversight for short-term and long-term objectives, contract negotiations, financial analysis and reporting, contract oversight, maintaining labor relations and strategic management of contract security services functions. With regards to professional certifications, he has attained the coveted Certified Protection Professional (CPP) status with ASIS International. He also holds the Certified in Homeland Security (CHS V) status with the American Board for Certification in Homeland Security. In addition, he is a board-certified Program Manager (CPM) with the International Association of Project and Program Managers.

Step 2: Understand Clearance Requirements Before the Solicitation Federal facility security contracts frequently require cleared officers — and the clearance level should be determined before solicitation, not after award. The Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) administers most federal personnel security investigations. Ask any prospective contractor how many currently-cleared officers they have available, at what clearance levels, and what their process is for maintaining clearance currency. Step 3: Examine the Supervision Ratio and On-Site Leadership Structure The ratio of supervisors to posted officers is one of the most reliable indicators of actual service quality — consistently underweighted in security proposals. Federal contracts specify minimum ratios in the Performance Work Statement, but these are floor requirements, not best practice. Our Supervisorial Training division trains supervisors specifically against each client’s post orders, not a generic certification curriculum. entries.answer: Most organizations discover their physical security gaps one of two ways: through a formal vulnerability assessment, or through an incident. The assessment is cheaper, faster, and produces a written remediation roadmap. The incident produces insurance claims, regulatory scrutiny, and questions about why the gap wasn’t addressed sooner. What Is a Physical Security Vulnerability Assessment? A physical security vulnerability assessment (PSVA) is a structured evaluation of physical protections measured against recognized threat scenarios and standards. Unlike an audit — which checks compliance against a specific standard — a PSVA answers three questions: What assets need protection? What are the credible threats? How well do current protections address those threats? ASIS International’s Physical Asset Protection standard (ASIS PAP) and the CISA Physical Security Performance Goals provide established frameworks that qualified assessors reference. Federal Continuity Directive 1 (FCD-1) requires all executive branch departments and agencies to maintain viable COOP capabilities. The challenge is not understanding the requirement — it is building a capability that actually works when needed, rather than a binder that satisfies an annual compliance review. The Eight Essential Elements FCD-1 Requires 1. Essential Functions Every COOP plan starts with identification of Mission Essential Functions (MEFs) and Primary Mission Essential Functions (PMEFs) — the subset of the agency’s work that must continue during a disruption. These must be specific and limited. An agency that declares every function “essential” has identified nothing useful for prioritization during an actual event. 2. Why Most COOP Exercises Fail The most common exercise failure mode is scripting: participants know the scenario in advance and “pass” by demonstrating what they were told to demonstrate. Effective exercises introduce realistic complications: Key personnel unavailability: Remove the primary person from the scenario and verify whether succession actually works System failures: Remove access to systems the plan assumes will be available Cascading disruptions: Layer secondary problems on top of the primary scenario to replicate real event complexity Time pressure: Impose realistic decision timelines rather than allowing indefinite deliberation After-action reports should be honest about what didn’t work. A COOP after-action report that finds no significant gaps is almost certainly not accurate. entries.answer: When a corporate board asks security leadership to “get a bodyguard for the CEO,” they usually mean something more sophisticated than the term implies — and the distinction matters operationally. A reactive, physically-focused close protection model leaves entirely different gaps than a proactive, intelligence-driven executive protection program. What “Bodyguard” Actually Means in Security A bodyguard’s primary function is physical interposition — being present to deter or physically block threats to the protected person. The model is reactive and visible. Its value lies in physical presence and the ability to respond when something goes wrong. This model has limited applications in corporate and government settings because it does not prevent threats — it responds to them. By the time a threat has progressed to the point where physical interposition is relevant, an intelligence failure has already occurred much earlier in the chain. entries.answer: Cleared security officer staffing sits at the intersection of two of the most administratively complex domains in federal contracting: physical security services and personnel security. The operational pressure of keeping posts staffed collides with the administrative reality that clearance processing is slow, unpredictable, and non-negotiable. Understanding both sides of that tension before a solicitation is drafted is what separates contracts that mobilize smoothly from ones that start with post vacancies and contracting officer complaints. DCSA Processing Timelines: What to Actually Plan Around The Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) administers personnel vetting for most federal departments and agencies outside the intelligence community. Current general planning timelines: Tier 1 (NACI — low-risk public trust): 3–6 weeks under normal workload Tier 2 (Moderate Risk Background Investigation): 2–4 months Tier 3 (Secret clearance): 3–6 months, complex cases longer Tier 5 (Top Secret clearance): Currently averaging 6–18 months depending on case complexity and adjudicative workload These are planning averages, not guarantees. Contracts that build staffing plans assuming clearance processing will complete within a specific timeline regularly fail to meet initial posting requirements. Plan for the upper end of the range; treat the lower end as a bonus. Interim

entries.answer: Clearances: What They Cover and Their Limits Interim clearances allow individuals to begin work in cleared positions while their full investigation is pending — but they are not universally available. Eligibility depends on: the investigation level requested, whether the investigation has been formally submitted and accepted by DCSA, whether there is any known derogatory information in the individual’s file, and agency-specific policies (some agencies do not grant interim access for security guard positions regardless of investigation status). Contracting officers should clarify in the Performance Work Statement whether interim clearances are acceptable for initial staffing, and what the timeline is for transitioning interim-cleared officers to full clearances. This language prevents ambiguity at mobilization when every day of delay has operational consequences. Best practice is to maintain a cleared bench — a pool of cleared officers exceeding the minimum staffing requirement — specifically to absorb CE-driven separations without going below minimum post coverage thresholds. NISPOM Requirements for Cleared Security Guard Programs The National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM) , codified at 32 CFR Part 117, is the primary governing document for cleared contractor operations. For security guard programs specifically, the NISPOM establishes requirements around: Visitor access control procedures at cleared facilities Badge and access control system management Security incident reporting requirements for guard-observed incidents Training requirements for security personnel with access to classified information Procedures for unauthorized disclosure or security violation reporting Guards at cleared facilities interacting with classified programs need to understand their specific NISPOM responsibilities — not just general security training. The integration between the security guard program and the facility security program is a common gap in facilities that contracted their guard force from a company whose primary expertise is not cleared contractor work. How does a clearance lapse affect a security officer’s ability to work on a cleared contract? A clearance that lapses due to administrative reasons (missed reinvestigation, failure to maintain employment in a cleared position, voluntary relinquishment) typically requires a new investigation — the prior investigation does not simply restart. Officers who leave cleared employment for more than 24 months generally cannot have their clearances reinstated; a new investigation is required. Maintaining clearance currency in a cleared position is therefore an important career consideration for security officers in the federal market. The Service Contract Act and Federal Security Pay Federal security service contracts are generally covered by the McNamara-O’Hara Service Contract Act (SCA) , administered by the Department of Labor. The SCA requires contractors to pay at least the prevailing wage and fringe benefits determined by DOL for the specific type of work and geographic location. In practice, this means security officers on federal contracts in the DC Metro earn more than counterparts on commercial contracts for equivalent work — often significantly more when the SCA’s health and welfare fringe benefit rate is included. A federal contract officer earning $28/hr plus the SCA H&W fringe benefit (currently over $5.00/hr) has total compensation well above what a $28/hr commercial officer receives. Understanding this comparison is important when evaluating employment offers. entries.answer: Specialized Division Personnel Security Our Personnel Security division manages the full lifecycle of clearance and credentialing work for federal and commercial clients. From initial background investigation through continuous evaluation, our team works hand-in-hand with security officers and facility security officers (FSOs) to keep sensitive positions properly vetted and documented to federal standard. We operate within NISPOM, DCSA, and PERSEC frameworks, and our case managers are experienced with the adjudicative guidelines used across federal agencies and cleared contractor environments. Whether you are standing up a new cleared workforce or maintaining an existing one, this division keeps the paperwork, the timelines, and the compliance posture in order. Core Capabilities Background investigation case management and tracking Security clearance adjudication liaison support Continuous evaluation and continuous vetting program design Insider threat program development and oversight Credentialing, badge issuance, and access tier management NISPOM / DCSA compliance documentation and audit readiness Clients typically engage this division alongside our Physical Security and Investigations services to build a complete personnel risk posture — from the first background check to ongoing insider threat monitoring. sources.title: About Us – Securemedy Nigeria Limited
sources.text: About Securemedy About Us On Time Response | Real Time Events To detect vulnerabilities, deter threats, and observe risks to our client's assets, report our findings, and suggest protective measures through superior security services. Our Mission Superior security, delivered on time. At Securemedy, Incorporated, we promise to take an aggressive approach to offering superior security solutions at a competitive cost. Our corporate motto is “On Time Response | Real Time Events”. To better serve you, we provide a superior level of service by assigning well-trained security professionals supervised by an experienced, educated and team-oriented corporate staff. This is a non-negotiable for each and every Securemedy Associate and our pledge to each and every one of our clients. About Us An emerging national leader in security. As of 2018, Securemedy Incorporated is now a full-scale security provider in 16 states and counting—two years ahead of schedule. We owe our success to the commitment and leadership of our “Chief” B.J. Folayan, as well as the men and women who have worked diligently on site and in our corporate office to make Securemedy an emerging national leader in the security industry. Securemedy Incorporated was founded as an “American-Owned” and “American-Managed”, diversified security services provider. 2009 Vision Founded as an American-Owned and American-Managed diversified security services provider, with a vision to become a reputable leader in providing diversified physical and electronic security services to public and private entities in at least 15 states by 2020. 2018 Realized A full-scale security provider in 16 states and counting — two years ahead of schedule. Leadership Meet Our Chairman Olabanji O. Folayan Chairman Certified Protection Professional (CPP), ASIS Board-Certified Project Manager (CPM), IAPM B.A. in Business, M.S. in Management, and a Graduate Certificate in Homeland Security Management, University of Maryland University College CHS-V designation through the American Board of Certification in Homeland Security 23 years of experience in various security and emergency management positions Olabanji O. Folayan was born and raised in the Washington Metropolitan Area, and attended the University of the District of Columbia (B.A., Business Administration 1997) and University of Maryland (M.S. Management 2004 and Graduate Certificate in Homeland Security Management 2007). Prior to establishing Securemedy, Incorporated, Mr. Folayan worked in various capacities from security officer to management, working on commercial and government contracts. He has provided oversight for a workforce of over 300 employees. His duties included management oversight for short-term and long-term objectives, contract negotiations, financial analysis and reporting, contract oversight, maintaining labor relations and strategic management of contract security services functions. With regards to professional certifications, he has attained the coveted Certified Protection Professional (CPP) status with ASIS International. He also holds the Certified in Homeland Security (CHS V) status with the American Board for Certification in Homeland Security. In addition, he is a board-certified Program Manager (CPM) with the International Association of Project and Program Managers. Affiliations Professional Memberships American Society for Industrial Security (A.S.I.S) International American Board for Certification in Homeland Security (A.B.C.H.S) International Association of Project and Program Management (I.A.P.P.M) Washington Area Security Managers Association (W.A.S.M.A) InfraGard Our success depends on people, never on a person.

Our personnel hold active state licenses and meet all federal security clearance requirements before they ever step onto a post. Posts are staffed to the client’s actual risk profile, not a one-size-fits-all template, and every officer reports through a chain of supervisors trained in our Supervisorial Training division — so the standard on post matches the standard in the post orders. sources.text: Effective Date: 06/16/2024 Privacy Policy Privacy Policy Effective Date: 06/16/2024 Welcome to Securemedy Incorporated’s Privacy Policy. Your privacy is important to us. This policy explains how we collect, use, and protect your personal data when you use our M3dyHub mobile application and our company website. Please read it carefully to understand our practices regarding your information. Information Collection and Use We collect two types of information: Personal Data: These are information that can be used to identify you, such as: i. Name ii. Email address iii. Profile information ​ iv. Phone Number Non-Personal Data: These are information that cannot be used to identify you, such as: i. Device operating system ii. Device type iii. Usage data iv. Analytics data How we use Personal Information We use your Personal Data to: i. Provide and enhance our Application and website ii. Notify you about updates and changes iii. Respond to your support requests iv. Comply with legal requirements We use Non-Personal Data to: i. Analyze usage trends ii. Improve our Application and Services iii. Provide targeted advertising with appropriate user consent Information Sharing We do not share your Personal Data with third parties for marketing purposes. With your consent we may share personal data with service providers who help us administer our services. Marketing and Consent We respect your privacy and will not use the collected data for unsolicited marketing purposes. You may opt out of receiving communication by following the instructions provided or by contacting us . Opt-Out: I have the right to opt-out of receiving SMS messages from Securemedy at any time. To do so, I can reply with “STOP” to any message received, or I can contact Securemedy’s HR department to request opt-out. No further messages will be sent after opting out. Data Security We implement reasonable security measures to protect your data from unauthorized access, disclosure, or misuse, including: i. Encryption ii. Firewalls iii. Secure servers iv. Access controls Data Retention We retain your data for as long as your account is active or as necessary for our services. . We may retain information as needed to comply with legal obligations or resolve disputes. User Rights You have rights concerning your Personal Data, including: i. Access and correction ii. Deletion or “Right to be forgotten” iii. Objection to processing iv. Restriction of processing v. Data Portability Policy Updates We may update this Privacy Policy periodically and will notify you of significant changes through updates on our Application and website. Contact Information For inquiries about this privacy policy, reach us at: i. itsupport.team@securemedy.com ii. info@securemedy.com Data Controller Securemedy Incorporated 8507 Oxon Hill Road Suit 101, Fort Washington MD 20744, USA. Data Protection Officer M3dyHub Team – itsupport.team[at]securemedy.com Compliance with Global Standards We adhere to global privacy standards, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), providing you with rights such as data access, correction, deletion, and portability. You may lodge a complaint with the appropriate data protection authority if necessary. Cookie Policy Our use of cookies enhances your experience on the Application and website. Manage your preference via browser settings. Third-Party Services We may use third-party services to support our Application and website which do not access your Personal Data without your explicit consent. Data Breach Notification In case of a data breach, we will notify affected individuals and the relevant authorities within defined timelines, in accordance with the applicable laws and regulations. App Store Compliance We comply with the privacy and data security standards required by Google Play Store and Apple Store ensuring protection of user’s data. Information Sharing Phone numbers or SMS consents are not shared with third parties for marketing purposes. All sharing of information is done in alignment with the user consent and legal requirements.

sources.title: How to Choose a Federal Security Contractor in Maryland, Virginia, and DC – Securemedy Nigeria Limited
sources.text: Selecting a security contractor for a federal facility or government-funded program is one of the highest-stakes procurement decisions a contracting officer makes. Get it wrong and you are managing constant staffing gaps and explaining compliance failures to agency leadership. This guide focuses on specific considerations for federal facilities and government-adjacent commercial properties in Maryland, Virginia, and Washington, DC — the densest concentration of federal contracting activity in the United States. Step 1: Verify State Licensing in Every State You Operate In Security guard licensing is state-by-state. A contractor licensed in Maryland cannot legally post officers in Virginia or DC without separate licenses. Before any vendor appears on your shortlist, confirm active guard agency licenses for every state where your facilities are located. In the Mid-Atlantic region, the relevant licensing bodies are: Maryland: Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services — maintains a public licensee search tool Virginia: Department of Criminal Justice Services (DCJS) — required for armed and unarmed guard agencies Washington, DC: Metropolitan Police Department Security Officers Management Branch (SOMB) Securemedy Incorporated holds active licenses in 16 states , including Maryland (106-4625), Virginia (11-6415), and DC (SAB 3242), and provides verification on request. Step 2: Understand Clearance Requirements Before the Solicitation Federal facility security contracts frequently require cleared officers — and the clearance level should be determined before solicitation, not after award. The Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) administers most federal personnel security investigations. Ask any prospective contractor how many currently-cleared officers they have available, at what clearance levels, and what their process is for maintaining clearance currency. Our Personnel Security service covers the full clearance lifecycle. Step 3: Examine the Supervision Ratio and On-Site Leadership Structure The ratio of supervisors to posted officers is one of the most reliable indicators of actual service quality — consistently underweighted in security proposals. Federal contracts specify minimum ratios in the Performance Work Statement, but these are floor requirements, not best practice. Our Supervisorial Training division trains supervisors specifically against each client’s post orders, not a generic certification curriculum. Step 4: Assess Staffing Depth and Vacancy Management Every vendor will say no-shows never happen. What you should evaluate is the system a contractor uses when they do. Ask: what is your bench size in this region? What is your average time-to-fill for a same-day vacancy? The Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System (CPARS) contains past performance ratings for federal contractors accessible to contracting officers during evaluation. Use it. Step 5: Verify Compliance Documentation and Insurance Federal security contracts require specific insurance coverages — typically comprehensive general liability, workers’ compensation, and an umbrella policy at minimum $1M per occurrence. Verify certificates of insurance directly against your PWS requirements, and confirm the government is listed as an additional insured. Ask to see a sample monthly compliance report — the format and completeness tells you more about administrative capability than any proposal. Past Performance Is the Strongest Predictor Request three recent references from federal contracts of comparable size and scope. Call them. Ask specifically about staffing reliability, supervisor responsiveness, documentation quality, and what happened the last time something went wrong on post. See how Securemedy has performed for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, U.S. Army Barnes Federal Building, and MIEMSS — with documented past performance across multiple assessment categories from contracting officers by name. Frequently Asked Questions What certifications should a federal security contractor hold? At minimum: active guard agency licenses in each state of operation, workers’ compensation and general liability insurance, and SAM.gov registration. Contractors pursuing 8(a) set-aside work need current SBA 8(a) Business Development Program certification. MBE, DBE, or SBE status expands contracting opportunities further. How long does it take to mobilize a federal security contract? Contracts requiring no clearances typically mobilize within 30–45 days of award. Secret-cleared contracts require 60–90 days for initial staffing. Top Secret or SCI contracts can require 6–18 months for full staffing if large numbers of new clearances must be initiated. Does a security contractor need to be local to serve a federal facility? Not strictly, but proximity matters operationally. A contractor with a management office and established cleared workforce within commuting distance will outperform a distant contractor every time there is a staffing vacancy or rapid-response requirement. Admin Security Intelligence Writer Providing expert analysis on federal security requirements, risk management practices, and emerging threats affecting government and commercial clients. Next SBA 8(a) Certified Security Contractors: What It Means and Why…

A contractor with a management office and established cleared workforce within commuting distance will outperform a distant contractor every time there is a staffing vacancy or rapid-response requirement. sources.title: Physical Security Vulnerability Assessments: What They Cover and How to Act on the Results – Securemedy Nigeria Limited
sources.text: Most organizations discover their physical security gaps one of two ways: through a formal vulnerability assessment, or through an incident. The assessment is cheaper, faster, and produces a written remediation roadmap. The incident produces insurance claims, regulatory scrutiny, and questions about why the gap wasn’t addressed sooner. What Is a Physical Security Vulnerability Assessment? A physical security vulnerability assessment (PSVA) is a structured evaluation of physical protections measured against recognized threat scenarios and standards. Unlike an audit — which checks compliance against a specific standard — a PSVA answers three questions: What assets need protection? What are the credible threats? How well do current protections address those threats? ASIS International’s Physical Asset Protection standard (ASIS PAP) and the CISA Physical Security Performance Goals provide established frameworks that qualified assessors reference. The Nine Domains Every PSVA Covers 1. Perimeter Security Fencing, vehicle barriers, lighting levels, line-of-sight from the street, and transition zones between public and controlled areas. Common finding: dark zones at shift change that are not covered by CCTV. 2. Entry Control How people and vehicles are screened before accessing the facility. Visitor management procedures, badge verification, tailgating vulnerability at turnstiles, and whether screening happens at all access points or only at the main entrance. 3. Access Control Technology Card reader systems, credential management, whether access rights are pruned regularly, and whether terminated employees are deprovisioned same-day. System age and manufacturer support status. 4. CCTV and Surveillance Camera coverage maps against the actual facility layout, image quality, recording retention, and monitoring frequency. Common finding: cameras are present but recorded footage is not useful for investigation because of insufficient resolution or retention periods. 5. Intrusion Detection Alarm systems, motion sensors, door contacts, and the response protocol when an alarm fires. What actually happens in the first five minutes after an after-hours intrusion alarm? 6. Security Staffing and Post Coverage Post orders, officer training, whether the post structure matches the facility’s risk profile, shift supervisor quality. How long would a post go uncovered before anyone noticed? 7. Policies and Procedures Whether written policies exist, are current, are known by officers and employees, and are tested. An outdated post order is frequently worse than no post order — it creates the appearance of process without the reality. 8. Emergency Response Mass notification, evacuation plans, shelter-in-place protocols, and coordination with local law enforcement and fire response. When were these last exercised and what were the after-action findings? 9. Insider Threat Indicators Not behavioral — procedural: are access rights commensurate with job function? Are there controls over high-value assets that would detect unauthorized access? Is there a mechanism to report concerning behavior? What Assessor Qualifications to Require Physical security assessment is not a regulated profession, so the quality range is wide. Look for assessors holding recognized credentials: Certified Protection Professional (CPP) or Physical Security Professional (PSP) from ASIS International, or prior law enforcement or military physical security experience. Ask to see redacted sample reports — the specificity of findings and rigor of recommendations reveal more than any credential list. Turning Findings Into Action The most common failure mode after a PSVA is the “binder on a shelf” outcome. To avoid it: assign an owner for each finding with a target date, sequence remediation by risk severity not by cost, budget long-term recommendations into the next capital cycle with the assessment as justification, and schedule a reassessment date (every 2–3 years for most facilities). Securemedy’s Risk Management service covers the full assessment lifecycle — from initial PSVA through remediation planning and follow-up validation. Review past projects from comparable facilities, and see our complete range of security services . FAQ Do federal facilities require physical security vulnerability assessments? Yes. Federal agencies are subject to the Interagency Security Committee (ISC) Risk Management Process , which requires periodic facility security assessments for all federal buildings, with frequency determined by the facility security level (FSL). How is a PSVA different from a security audit? An audit checks compliance against a specific standard and produces pass/fail findings. A PSVA evaluates overall effectiveness against actual threat scenarios. Most mature programs benefit from both: periodic audits to maintain standards and periodic PSVAs to evaluate effectiveness against evolving threats. sources.title: Armed Security Guard Licensing Requirements in Maryland, Virginia, and Washington DC – Securemedy Nigeria Limited
sources.text: Security officers who carry firearms in the DC Metro area face a patchwork of state and local licensing requirements that trip up both employers and individual officers who assume one state’s license transfers to another. It doesn’t. An officer fully licensed in Maryland cannot legally carry on post in Virginia or DC until they separately meet those jurisdictions’ requirements. Maryland Armed Security Officer Licensing Maryland security guard licensing is administered by the Maryland Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services . For armed officers, Maryland requires: Basic training: Minimum 16 hours of pre-assignment training covering legal aspects, emergency procedures, reporting, and safety Armed training: Additional firearms training certified by the Maryland Police Training and Standards Commission, including classroom instruction and live-fire qualification Annual firearms qualification: Officers must achieve a passing score on an approved range qualification course, renewed annually Background check: Criminal background investigation through the Maryland State Police and FBI Dual licensing: Both the employer agency and the individual officer must be licensed — agencies hold a company license number; individual officers hold separate registration cards Agency licenses renew every two years; individual registration cards renew annually and require confirmation of current firearms qualification. Virginia Armed Security Officer Licensing Virginia regulates armed security officers through the Department of Criminal Justice Services (DCJS) under Virginia Code § 9.1-138 et seq. Virginia requires significantly more structured training than most states: Entry Level Training (ELT): 18 hours of classroom instruction covering topics specified in 6VAC20-171-60, including legal limitations, emergency procedures, and public relations Armed Security Officer training: An additional 16 hours specific to armed operations, plus a firearms qualification Annual requalification: Officers must qualify on an approved course at minimum annually Virginia DCJS registration: Individual registration required before an officer can provide armed services — registration card must be in the officer’s possession while on duty Renewal: Every two years, requiring documentation of continuing education training hours Washington DC Armed Security Officer Licensing DC regulates security officers through the Metropolitan Police Department’s Security Officers Management Branch (SOMB) under the Security Officers Study Act (D.C. Code § 47-2853.01 et seq.). DC’s requirements are among the most stringent in the region: Pre-assignment training: Minimum 24 hours before an officer may work their first post Annual in-service training: DC requires ongoing annual training hours to maintain registration — not just at initial licensing Armed endorsement: Officers who carry firearms must obtain a separate armed endorsement with additional training and qualification DC firearms laws: DC has specific carrying requirements more restrictive than federal law — armed officers must be thoroughly familiar with DC Code § 22-4501 and related provisions Agency license required: The security company must hold a DC security agency license before any officer may work in DC Carrying Across Jurisdictions: The Critical Compliance Gap Armed security officers in the DC Metro area often work assignments crossing jurisdictional lines. In these situations, the officer must be licensed in every jurisdiction where they carry a firearm on duty. A Virginia-licensed officer who briefly enters DC while on armed patrol without DC authorization is in violation of DC law — and the employer is responsible for ensuring all officers hold correct credentials before deployment. This is one of the most common compliance failures in the DC Metro security market. When evaluating armed security contractors, ask specifically for a list of the jurisdictions where their armed officers are currently licensed, and cross-reference it against your facility locations. How Securemedy Manages Licensing Compliance Securemedy maintains an internal compliance tracking system monitoring license and registration expiration dates for every officer across all 16 states where we operate. No officer is deployed on an armed post without a current registration in the relevant jurisdiction confirmed in our system. Our Personnel Security and Physical Security teams coordinate to ensure every post has officers meeting the specific licensing requirements for that location. If you are building a security contract in the DC Metro area and need current license verification documentation, our operations team can provide it within 24 hours of request. Frequently Asked Questions Can a Maryland-licensed armed security officer work in Virginia without additional licensing? No. Maryland and Virginia have separate licensing regimes with no reciprocity. An officer must independently meet Virginia DCJS armed security officer training and registration requirements before carrying a firearm on duty in Virginia. How long does it take to license a new armed security officer in the DC Metro area? An officer starting from zero who needs licensure in all three jurisdictions (Maryland, Virginia, and DC) should plan for 6–12 weeks minimum, accounting for background investigation processing time, scheduled training course availability, and application processing at each licensing authority. What happens if an officer is caught working armed without the correct jurisdiction’s license? Both the officer and the employing security agency can face criminal charges, civil penalties, and license suspension or revocation. In DC specifically, unlicensed armed security work can constitute illegal carrying of a dangerous weapon under DC Code. sources.title: COOP Planning for Federal Agencies and Contractors: What FCD-1 Actually Requires – Securemedy Nigeria Limited
sources.text: Continuity of Operations (COOP) planning is not optional for federal agencies. Federal Continuity Directive 1 (FCD-1) requires all executive branch departments and agencies to maintain viable COOP capabilities. The challenge is not understanding the requirement — it is building a capability that actually works when needed, rather than a binder that satisfies an annual compliance review. The Eight Essential Elements FCD-1 Requires 1. Essential Functions Every COOP plan starts with identification of Mission Essential Functions (MEFs) and Primary Mission Essential Functions (PMEFs) — the subset of the agency’s work that must continue during a disruption. These must be specific and limited. An agency that declares every function “essential” has identified nothing useful for prioritization during an actual event. 2. Succession of Authority Who takes over each leadership role if the primary official is unavailable, and in what order? Successions must go at least three deep for each key position, identified by position rather than by name alone — individuals change; positions persist. 3. Delegation of Authority Delegations must be explicit, pre-authorized, and legally sufficient. An official who has not been delegated authority in advance cannot be assumed to have it during an emergency. Review your delegation framework with legal counsel before the plan is finalized. 4. Alternate Facilities Where will essential functions be performed if the primary facility is unavailable? Alternate facilities must be identified, equipped, and tested. “We will work from home” is not a viable COOP alternate facility solution for operations requiring secure systems, classified information, or specialized equipment. 5. Communications How will leadership communicate with staff, other agencies, and the public during a disruption that affects primary systems? COOP communications plans must address scenarios where email, phone, and VPN are unavailable — which is precisely when communication is most critical. 6. Vital Records Management Which records are necessary for essential functions? Where are they stored? How current are the backups? How quickly can they be accessed from the alternate facility? Records inaccessible from the alternate site are effectively unavailable during a primary facility disruption. 7. Human Capital Which personnel are required for essential functions? Are they trained on their COOP roles? Do they know what to do without being told? Effective human capital planning goes beyond identifying names to ensuring individuals can execute their roles under pressure without step-by-step instruction. 8. Tests, Training, and Exercises FCD-1 requires annual testing and training. This is the element most often treated as a check-the-box exercise — a scripted tabletop that concludes the plan works without testing any systems or procedures. This is also the element where the most value is destroyed by minimal compliance. Why Most COOP Exercises Fail The most common exercise failure mode is scripting: participants know the scenario in advance and “pass” by demonstrating what they were told to demonstrate. Effective exercises introduce realistic complications: Key personnel unavailability: Remove the primary person from the scenario and verify whether succession actually works System failures: Remove access to systems the plan assumes will be available Cascading disruptions: Layer secondary problems on top of the primary scenario to replicate real event complexity Time pressure: Impose realistic decision timelines rather than allowing indefinite deliberation After-action reports should be honest about what didn’t work. A COOP after-action report that finds no significant gaps is almost certainly not accurate. What Federal Contractors Need to Know Federal contractors often assume their agency clients’ COOP plans cover contractor personnel and systems. In most cases, they do not. Contractors are expected to maintain their own business continuity capabilities for continued contract performance during disruptions — particularly on mission-critical contracts. Review your contracts for continuity of performance language. These provisions are commonly unread and uncomplied-with at award. Securemedy’s Emergency Management Support Our Emergency Management service and Emergency Management division support federal agencies across the full COOP lifecycle: plan development, staff training, tabletop exercises, full-scale drills, Emergency Operations Center (EOC) staffing during real activations, and after-action report development with honest gap identification. See the U.S. Army Barnes Federal Building past project — where Securemedy maintained uninterrupted security services through a multi-year COVID-19 disruption with zero coverage gaps, receiving formal written recommendations from the Contracting Officer across multiple performance categories. For authoritative source material, see Federal Continuity Directive 1 (FCD-1) and FEMA’s COOP resources page . Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between a COOP plan and a Disaster Recovery plan? A COOP plan focuses on maintaining essential functions during any disruption — it is people, process, and location continuity. A Disaster Recovery plan focuses on restoring technical systems and IT infrastructure after failure. Both are necessary, but they address different aspects of organizational resilience. COOP plans should reference DR plans for the technology recovery timeline, but COOP cannot be reduced to an IT recovery procedure. How often must federal agencies test their COOP plans? FCD-1 requires annual testing and training of COOP capabilities at minimum. Many agencies conduct more frequent exercises based on risk profile. After any significant facility change, leadership transition, or real-world activation, a supplemental exercise to validate the updated plan is best practice. Are COOP exercises required to involve the alternate facility? FCD-1 requires that agencies periodically conduct full tests that include activation of the alternate facility. Annual tabletop exercises at the primary facility do not satisfy the full-test requirement. A realistic cadence for most agencies is annual tabletop plus biennial or triennial full activation test at the alternate facility. Tests, Training, and Exercises FCD-1 requires annual testing and training. This is the element most often treated as a check-the-box exercise — a scripted tabletop that concludes the plan works without testing any systems or procedures. This is also the element where the most value is destroyed by minimal compliance. Why Most COOP Exercises Fail The most common exercise failure mode is scripting: participants know the scenario in advance and “pass” by demonstrating what they were told to demonstrate. Effective exercises introduce realistic complications: Key personnel unavailability: Remove the primary person from the scenario and verify whether succession actually works System failures: Remove access to systems the plan assumes will be available Cascading disruptions: Layer secondary problems on top of the primary scenario to replicate real event complexity Time pressure: Impose realistic decision timelines rather than allowing indefinite deliberation After-action reports should be honest about what didn’t work. A COOP after-action report that finds no significant gaps is almost certainly not accurate. What Federal Contractors Need to Know Federal contractors often assume their agency clients’ COOP plans cover contractor personnel and systems. In most cases, they do not. Contractors are expected to maintain their own business continuity capabilities for continued contract performance during disruptions — particularly on mission-critical contracts. Review your contracts for continuity of performance language. These provisions are commonly unread and uncomplied-with at award. Securemedy’s Emergency Management Support Our Emergency Management service and Emergency Management division support federal agencies across the full COOP lifecycle: plan development, staff training, tabletop exercises, full-scale drills, Emergency Operations Center (EOC) staffing during real activations, and after-action report development with honest gap identification. See the U.S. Army Barnes Federal Building past project — where Securemedy maintained uninterrupted security services through a multi-year COVID-19 disruption with zero coverage gaps, receiving formal written recommendations from the Contracting Officer across multiple performance categories. For authoritative source material, see Federal Continuity Directive 1 (FCD-1) and FEMA’s COOP resources page . Frequently Asked Questions What is the difference between a COOP plan and a Disaster Recovery plan? A COOP plan focuses on maintaining essential functions during any disruption — it is people, process, and location continuity. A Disaster Recovery plan focuses on restoring technical systems and IT infrastructure after failure. Both are necessary, but they address different aspects of organizational resilience. COOP plans should reference DR plans for the technology recovery timeline, but COOP cannot be reduced to an IT recovery procedure. How often must federal agencies test their COOP plans? FCD-1 requires annual testing and training of COOP capabilities at minimum. Many agencies conduct more frequent exercises based on risk profile. After any significant facility change, leadership transition, or real-world activation, a supplemental exercise to validate the updated plan is best practice. Are COOP exercises required to involve the alternate facility? FCD-1 requires that agencies periodically conduct full tests that include activation of the alternate facility. Annual tabletop exercises at the primary facility do not satisfy the full-test requirement. A realistic cadence for most agencies is annual tabletop plus biennial or triennial full activation test at the alternate facility. sources.title: Executive Protection vs. Bodyguard: Key Differences and Which One Your Organization Actually Needs – Securemedy Nigeria Limited
sources.text: When a corporate board asks security leadership to “get a bodyguard for the CEO,” they usually mean something more sophisticated than the term implies — and the distinction matters operationally. A reactive, physically-focused close protection model leaves entirely different gaps than a proactive, intelligence-driven executive protection program. What “Bodyguard” Actually Means in Security A bodyguard’s primary function is physical interposition — being present to deter or physically block threats to the protected person. The model is reactive and visible. Its value lies in physical presence and the ability to respond when something goes wrong. This model has limited applications in corporate and government settings because it does not prevent threats — it responds to them. By the time a threat has progressed to the point where physical interposition is relevant, an intelligence failure has already occurred much earlier in the chain. What Executive Protection Actually Involves Executive protection (EP) is a proactive, systems-based approach that treats threat prevention as the primary objective and physical response as a last resort. A competent EP program involves: Advance Work Before a principal moves to any location — a hotel, an event venue, an airport terminal — an advance agent surveys the location for threat factors, identifies entry and exit routes, locates medical facilities, and establishes emergency protocols. The advance is the work that prevents incidents from ever reaching the close protection team. Threat Assessment A current, maintained threat picture for the principal, including known persons of concern, travel-specific risks, and geopolitical factors relevant to international movement. A static briefing from six months ago is a historical document, not a threat assessment. Route Planning and Secure Transportation Primary and alternate routes to every destination, accounting for traffic patterns, protest activity, and known threat environments. Defensive and evasive driving capability. Vehicle inspection protocols. In higher-threat contexts, motorcade procedures. Residential Security For principals with home security requirements: perimeter assessment, visitor protocols, staff vetting, and residential security officer deployment where warranted by threat level. Coordination With Venue and Facility Security EP details do not operate in isolation. They coordinate with security at every location the principal visits, with event security teams, and where appropriate with law enforcement liaisons. A detail that treats itself as self-contained creates gaps at every handoff point. When Is Executive Protection Warranted? Organizations that haven’t previously engaged professional EP consistently underestimate when it is warranted. Indicators include: The principal is a public figure whose name and schedule are known to a broad audience The organization has received credible threats directed at leadership The principal travels to locations with elevated risk profiles The principal’s decisions affect large numbers of people in ways that could generate adversarial sentiment (regulatory enforcement, major litigation, significant workforce reductions) Geopolitical factors create elevated risk for industry-specific executives in energy, defense, financial services, or government affairs sectors The Bureau of Labor Statistics classifies executive protection agents under a distinct occupational category from security guards precisely because the skill set, training, and operational context are fundamentally different. The career path, compensation, and competency requirements don’t overlap as much as the general public assumes. What to Ask When Evaluating EP Providers The most important differentiator is experience with advance work and threat assessment — not physical appearance. Specific questions that reveal capability: Describe your advance protocol for a domestic business travel assignment. How many days in advance does it begin? What specifically do you assess at each location? How do you maintain a current threat picture for a principal over an extended engagement? Describe the last time something in an advance changed your recommendation for how the principal traveled. What changed and why? What medical training do your agents carry? (First-responder capability is a minimum expectation for any professional EP team.) How do you coordinate with event security teams and venue management for large appearances? How Securemedy Handles Executive Protection Our Executive Protection division handles engagements from single-agent domestic travel coverage through full multi-agent advance and motorcade operations for visiting principals. Concierge Services complements EP for venue-based events where a hospitality-trained presence alongside protective coverage is appropriate — ensuring the welcome at the front desk never comes at the cost of security. See our past project portfolio including coordinated protection for a multi-day diplomatic conference with attending foreign dignitaries, where Securemedy’s Executive Protection division coordinated daily K9 sweeps, close protection details, and integration with federal law enforcement partners — zero incidents across all three days. Frequently Asked Questions Does executive protection require a private investigator license in Maryland or Virginia? In Maryland and Virginia, executive protection agents providing close protection services typically need to be registered under the respective state’s security guard licensing framework, not as private investigators. The specific licensing pathway depends on the precise scope of services provided. Legal review of the specific service scope is advisable before deploying EP agents in any new jurisdiction. What is the difference between EP and armed security for executives? Armed security officers on fixed posts protect locations. Executive protection agents protect a person in motion — across multiple locations, environments, and threat contexts. Armed capability is one element of EP, but an armed officer with no advance work experience and no threat assessment capability is not providing executive protection regardless of how they are billed. sources.title: Staffing Cleared Security Personnel for Federal Contracts: A Guide for Contracting Officers and FSOs – Securemedy Nigeria Limited
sources.text: Cleared security officer staffing sits at the intersection of two of the most administratively complex domains in federal contracting: physical security services and personnel security. The operational pressure of keeping posts staffed collides with the administrative reality that clearance processing is slow, unpredictable, and non-negotiable. Understanding both sides of that tension before a solicitation is drafted is what separates contracts that mobilize smoothly from ones that start with post vacancies and contracting officer complaints. DCSA Processing Timelines: What to Actually Plan Around The Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) administers personnel vetting for most federal departments and agencies outside the intelligence community. Current general planning timelines: Tier 1 (NACI — low-risk public trust): 3–6 weeks under normal workload Tier 2 (Moderate Risk Background Investigation): 2–4 months Tier 3 (Secret clearance): 3–6 months, complex cases longer Tier 5 (Top Secret clearance): Currently averaging 6–18 months depending on case complexity and adjudicative workload These are planning averages, not guarantees. Contracts that build staffing plans assuming clearance processing will complete within a specific timeline regularly fail to meet initial posting requirements. Plan for the upper end of the range; treat the lower end as a bonus. Interim Clearances: What They Cover and Their Limits Interim clearances allow individuals to begin work in cleared positions while their full investigation is pending — but they are not universally available. Eligibility depends on: the investigation level requested, whether the investigation has been formally submitted and accepted by DCSA, whether there is any known derogatory information in the individual’s file, and agency-specific policies (some agencies do not grant interim access for security guard positions regardless of investigation status). Contracting officers should clarify in the Performance Work Statement whether interim clearances are acceptable for initial staffing, and what the timeline is for transitioning interim-cleared officers to full clearances. This language prevents ambiguity at mobilization when every day of delay has operational consequences. Continuous Evaluation: The New Staffing Risk Factor The Continuous Evaluation (CE) program automatically monitors cleared individuals between periodic reinvestigations for financial data, criminal records, and other indicators that might affect clearance eligibility. CE creates an important operational reality: a currently-cleared officer whose clearance was valid at their last reinvestigation may have their access suspended or revoked at any point if CE produces a derogatory finding. A staffing plan that doesn’t account for unplanned CE-driven clearance suspensions will be caught short. Best practice is to maintain a cleared bench — a pool of cleared officers exceeding the minimum staffing requirement — specifically to absorb CE-driven separations without going below minimum post coverage thresholds. NISPOM Requirements for Cleared Security Guard Programs The National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM) , codified at 32 CFR Part 117, is the primary governing document for cleared contractor operations. For security guard programs specifically, the NISPOM establishes requirements around: Visitor access control procedures at cleared facilities Badge and access control system management Security incident reporting requirements for guard-observed incidents Training requirements for security personnel with access to classified information Procedures for unauthorized disclosure or security violation reporting Guards at cleared facilities interacting with classified programs need to understand their specific NISPOM responsibilities — not just general security training. The integration between the security guard program and the facility security program is a common gap in facilities that contracted their guard force from a company whose primary expertise is not cleared contractor work. How Securemedy Manages Cleared Guard Staffing Securemedy’s Personnel Security service manages the clearance lifecycle for all cleared officers we deploy — from initial investigation submission through continuous evaluation monitoring and periodic reinvestigation initiation. We maintain a cleared staffing bench sized to absorb clearance losses without impacting post coverage. Our FSO maintains direct coordination with DCSA and can brief client FSOs on current case status for any officer in our cleared workforce. Our track record on multi-year federal contracts — including U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and U.S. Army Barnes Federal Building — demonstrates sustained performance on cleared contracts over extended periods with documented contractor officer satisfaction ratings. Frequently Asked Questions What clearance level is most commonly required for federal security guard contracts? Most federal facility security guard contracts require Secret clearances or public trust investigations (Tier 1 or Tier 2), with Top Secret requirements reserved for facilities handling classified programs or sensitive compartmented information. The specific requirement should be determined by the agency’s FSO and Contracting Officer based on the facility’s security level and the nature of classified activity present. Can security contractors initiate clearance investigations themselves? Yes. Cleared contractor companies (including security guard companies) can sponsor clearance investigations for their employees through DISS (Defense Information System for Security) if they hold a facility clearance (FCL). The company must hold an FCL appropriate to the clearance level being requested. Securemedy holds an active FCL enabling us to sponsor and manage clearance investigations for our officers directly. How does a clearance lapse affect a security officer’s ability to work on a cleared contract? A clearance that lapses due to administrative reasons (missed reinvestigation, failure to maintain employment in a cleared position, voluntary relinquishment) typically requires a new investigation — the prior investigation does not simply restart. Officers who leave cleared employment for more than 24 months generally cannot have their clearances reinstated; a new investigation is required. Maintaining clearance currency in a cleared position is therefore an important career consideration for security officers in the federal market. sources.text: The security plan for a corporate conference, government gala, or high-profile fundraiser should not be finalized the week before the event. By that point the venue is contracted, the guest list is confirmed, invitations are sent, and the program is committed — and every one of those decisions has security implications that the security team should have had input on before they were locked in. Phase 1: Initial Risk Assessment (6–12 Weeks Before) A special events risk assessment evaluates three factors in combination: the nature of the event and its attendees, the venue’s security environment, and the contextual threat landscape at the time of the event. Attendee and Event Assessment Who is attending, and are any attendees likely targets for threats? Events with government officials, executives, activists, or other high-profile attendees face different threat profiles than general public events. Has the organization or any of its principals received threats recently? Are there protest groups who might target attendees or the organization? Venue Assessment The security team should conduct a physical survey of every event space: entry points, access control locations, sight lines, emergency exits, staging areas, perimeter access, service entrances, vehicle approach zones, and the distance from public access to the event space. Venue surveys should happen when the security team has input on venue selection — not after the contract is signed. Contextual Threat Landscape What is the current threat environment in the event location? The DHS National Terrorism Advisory System (NTAS) reflects the current federal assessment of domestic threat conditions. Does the event fall near a politically sensitive date? Are there planned demonstrations in the event area? Have recent incidents occurred at similar events? Phase 2: Security Plan Development (4–8 Weeks Before) The security plan is a written document covering: Staffing plan: Officers by role and location, supervisor structure, shift timing, and briefing schedule Access control procedures: Credentialing system, screening processes, vendor and media access protocols, VIP procedures Communication plan: Radio channels, command structure, contact lists for venue management, law enforcement, and event production Emergency action plan: Evacuation procedures, shelter-in-place protocols, medical emergency response, and armed threat response VIP and dignitary protection: If any VIPs are attending, how do they move through the event? What additional protection is in place? Crowd flow management: Entry queue management, capacity monitoring, and contingency if attendance exceeds venue capacity This plan should be shared with venue management, event production, and local law enforcement in advance — not handed to them on the day of the event. A security team that plans an event in isolation from local law enforcement, then calls 911 when something goes wrong, has failed a basic planning obligation. The shift briefing covers: the event program and schedule, the communication plan, the emergency action plan, known VIPs or persons of concern, and last-minute changes from venue or production. Throughout the event, security supervisors maintain active radio contact with all post positions, event production, and the venue operations center. Any deviation from planned crowd flow or access patterns should be flagged and assessed in real time — not reported after the event in an incident log. Phase 5: After-Action Debrief (Within 72 Hours) A written after-action report should cover: what worked as planned, what deviated and why, any incidents and how they were handled, and recommendations for future events at the same venue or with the same client. After-action reports are most commonly skipped for events where “nothing happened” — which is exactly when they are most valuable for building a replicable security template. K9 Detection Services provides pre-event sweeps for large or elevated-risk events, and the Executive Protection division handles VIP and dignitary protection coordination. See the diplomatic conference past project — a multi-day event with foreign dignitaries where Securemedy coordinated daily K9 sweeps, close protection details for attending principals, and real-time liaison with federal law enforcement partners, resulting in zero security incidents across all three days. For general emergency preparedness planning resources, Ready.gov publishes public guidance that complements professional event security planning. Frequently Asked Questions How far in advance should I engage a security company for a major corporate event? For events of 200+ attendees with any VIP presence, engage your security provider at least 8–12 weeks in advance. This allows time for a venue assessment while there is still flexibility in access control planning, law enforcement coordination that gives the relevant precinct adequate notice, staffing plans that don’t depend on last-minute officer sourcing, and a credentialing system that is set up and tested before the day of the event. What size event requires professional security versus relying on venue staff? Venue security staff are trained for the venue’s specific environment and their primary responsibility is the venue — not the event or its specific attendees. Any event with distinguishable VIPs, a guest list requiring credentialing beyond ticket scanning, any elevated threat profile, or attendance above the venue’s comfortable staffing capacity warrants professional security beyond venue staff alone. These categories cover most corporate and government events of meaningful size. sources.text: Security in a healthcare environment is fundamentally different from security in a commercial office building. The population entering a hospital or medical practice includes people who are frightened, in pain, or grieving — factors that increase behavioral escalation probability in ways security officers must be trained to anticipate and de-escalate, not just react to. At the same time, the healthcare setting imposes constraints that don’t exist elsewhere: HIPAA, Joint Commission accreditation standards, and the need to maintain a calm, welcoming environment while running meaningful security controls. The Security Challenges Unique to Healthcare Workplace Violence Risk Healthcare workers face a disproportionate rate of workplace violence compared to other industries. OSHA’s workplace violence data consistently shows healthcare workers experiencing physical assault at rates 4–5 times higher than the national average across all industries. Emergency departments carry the highest risk, but inpatient units, psychiatric facilities, and outpatient behavioral health settings also present elevated exposure. Security programs in healthcare settings must specifically address workplace violence prevention and response — not just access control. Officers need training in recognizing pre-assault behavioral indicators, verbal de-escalation techniques appropriate for medically and psychiatrically compromised individuals, and hands-on restraint appropriate to a healthcare setting (different from general security use-of-force protocols). 24/7 Operations With Variable Risk Profiles Hospitals never close. Night and weekend shifts face different risk profiles than daytime operations — different patient populations, reduced staffing across the facility, lower lighting in isolated areas, and different visitor patterns. Staffing levels and post configurations that adequately cover the day shift often leave the overnight environment under-resourced. HIPAA and Privacy Obligations for Security Personnel HIPAA’s Privacy Rule restricts access to protected health information (PHI) — and security officers in healthcare routinely encounter PHI. Security cameras in patient care areas, visitor logs that include patient information, and incident reports referencing patient status all create HIPAA obligations security vendors must understand and comply with. Healthcare organizations are responsible for training their security contractors on HIPAA obligations. Security contractors who don’t acknowledge these obligations in service agreements create compliance risk for their clients. The HHS HIPAA Security Rule is the authoritative reference, and HHS’s guidance on business associates is directly applicable to security companies working in healthcare settings. Joint Commission Environment of Care Standards Accredited hospitals must meet the Joint Commission’s Environment of Care (EC) standards , which include specific requirements around security management planning, security incident documentation, access control, and the hospital’s approach to security-sensitive areas. Security vendors must be familiar with these standards and support the hospital’s compliance documentation process — not just perform their post assignments in isolation from the accreditation framework. What Healthcare Security Programs Actually Require De-escalation Training as a Core Competency The first response to a behavioral incident in a healthcare setting should almost never be physical. Officers who default to physical control as a first response in a hospital create liability, disrupt care, and frequently escalate the situation. De-escalation training specific to healthcare populations — including patients with dementia, acute psychiatric presentations, and substance withdrawal — should be a documented minimum competency for any officer deployed in a healthcare environment, not an optional add-on. Visitor Management at Scale Large healthcare facilities process thousands of visitors per day. Visitor management systems requiring individual officer screening for every visitor don’t scale. An effective healthcare visitor management program combines technology (visitor management software, badge printing, integration with the electronic health record’s visitor policy flags) with security officer oversight at pinch points. After-Hours Staff Escort Services Staff working late shifts — particularly in parking structures and isolated areas — face elevated risk. Escort services for after-hours departing staff are a basic safety measure that demonstrably improves retention in healthcare environments where safety concerns are a documented driver of staff turnover. Patient Elopement Prevention For inpatient facilities and emergency departments, patient elopement (unauthorized departure) is a safety and liability concern requiring defined security protocols. How are elopement attempts managed? What response is triggered? How are elopement incidents documented? These questions should have written post order answers, not improvisational responses. Securemedy’s Healthcare Security Experience in Maryland Securemedy has served multiple healthcare clients in Maryland, including Community Radiology Associates in Waldorf and the Maryland Institute for Emergency Medical Services Systems (MIEMSS) in Baltimore. Both engagements required understanding healthcare-specific constraints and risk profiles. See the MIEMSS past project — where Securemedy’s services were specifically cited as “an asset to MIEMSS” by the Agency Director, who noted officers were “professional, well-trained and personable.” And the Community Radiology Associates engagement , where the Practice Administrator cited “peace of mind knowing when I left for the evening that my staff would be well taken care of and looked after.” Our Physical Security and Concierge Services are deployed in healthcare settings with healthcare-specific training protocols. We are actively recruiting security professionals with healthcare facility experience in the Mid-Atlantic region. Frequently Asked Questions Are security guards in Maryland hospitals required to have any healthcare-specific training? Maryland state licensing does not currently mandate healthcare-specific training beyond the standard armed/unarmed guard pre-assignment curriculum. However, Joint Commission accreditation standards require hospitals to define and document the competencies required for security personnel, including healthcare-specific de-escalation and patient management. In practice, this means accredited Maryland hospitals should be specifying healthcare-specific training requirements in their security service agreements even where state law doesn’t mandate it. Can healthcare security officers physically restrain patients? This is a clinically and legally complex area that varies by state, facility policy, and the specific circumstances of the situation. In Maryland, physical restraint of patients is subject to both state regulations and Joint Commission standards that require clinical involvement in restraint decisions. Security officers in healthcare settings should have written facility-specific protocols covering when and how they may assist clinical staff with restraint situations, developed with the facility’s legal, clinical, and risk management teams. Security officers should not develop these protocols independently.
